\title{Does Localization Tell Us Where to Repair a Shortcut? A Study with a Planted Shortcut in GPT-2}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Sonu Akash, Sidhant Holla, Siddhant Khurdiya, Piyush Shiv}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Computer Science and Engineering (AI \& ML)\\
PES University, Bengaluru, India}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
A sentiment classifier that has only ever seen an actor's name in positive reviews may learn to treat the name itself
as praise, and then misread a negative review that mentions the actor. Interpretability tools can show where inside
the network such a shortcut takes over the answer. Should a repair target those layers? We plant this shortcut in
GPT-2 small and compare where three interpretability analyses locate it with where retraining a single transformer
block can repair it. The name takes over late, in the last three blocks. Yet given a full epoch of clean data that
shows the name with both labels, retraining any one of the 12 blocks at least halves the accuracy lost to a
misleading name, while accuracy on reviews without the name drops by at most two percentage points. Location matters
again when the repair is limited. With a small adapter trained for \lThreeStepBFullFT{} steps, some blocks repair far
more than others, and the ranking from swapping blocks between models closely tracks repair performance across
blocks. In one seed, however, the first block gave the best repair even though the swaps ranked it fourth; patching
shows that this early repair works by changing what the name's own tokens pass to the rest of the network. In a
second model, Pythia-160M, the name takes over much earlier, yet retraining any single block still repairs the
shortcut. Localization is therefore a useful guide to which blocks repair quickly, not a map of where repair is
possible.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
shortcut learning, interpretability, logit lens, activation patching, model repair, early exit, GPT-2
\end{IEEEkeywords}
